sources.note: Full 19-min transcript read to the end.

sources.title: Why Software Factories Fail (ai.engineer talk page, article form)
sources.note: Third-party-written article layered on the talk; used for chapters and resource list; ideas carded only where the transcript backs them.

sources.title: Conffab AIEWF day-1 keynotes session transcript
sources.note: Truncated: ends mid program-design section; no slides. Duplicate of the YouTube transcript for the part it covers.

sources.title: The Great Loops Debate (YouTube auto-caption transcript)
sources.note: Full transcript read; no speaker labels, Dex's turns identified by content and moderator cues.

sources.title: The Great Loops Debate (ai.engineer talk page, article form)
sources.note: Chaptered write-up; used to cross-check Dex's positions and the context-budget table.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: no amount of harness engineering or loops maxing can solve what is fundamentally a model training issue
cards.claim: Harness engineering and more loops cannot fix the missing maintainability signal in model training, so the harness alone is not enough.
cards.evidence_detail: Argument from how RL rewards are built; no experiment of his own.
cards.landing: Framing for the review: harness checks (refuters, gates) lift the floor but are not a substitute for owner reading of code.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: pull request code review quality is way down
cards.claim: A Faros AI report shows more and longer review comments, PRs merged with no review, and incidents and bugs per developer up since AI tools were adopted.
cards.evidence_detail: Cites the Faros AI report on a slide; no figures spoken; the page notes it is not proof of causation.
cards.landing: Supports keeping a human review step in the phase routine and the one-page owner view.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: agents really start to struggle after maybe 3 to 6 months
cards.claim: In fast-moving codebases agents begin to struggle after roughly three to six months of agent-driven change, not only in ten-year-old legacy code.
cards.evidence_detail: Own experience at HumanLayer; no numbers beyond the 3 to 6 month estimate.
cards.landing: Relevant to cold-resume trial (P1): FixFlow is months into agent-heavy change; resume-from-repo ability is the thing at risk.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: in July 2025, we tried this. We went full lights off
cards.claim: HumanLayer ran fully lights-off (no code reading) in July 2025 and later had to debug unread code during an outage with a down site and angry users.
cards.evidence_detail: First-hand story: an issue resisted advanced prompting, research and reproduction; the team had to dig into code it stopped reading three months earlier.
cards.landing: Justification for owner reading of diffs; argues against dropping the per-PR reviewer and owner view.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: they can't maintain and improve code base quality over time, not without a decent amount of human steering
cards.claim: Models cannot maintain or improve codebase quality over time without substantial human steering, and he thinks they have not improved at this since 2025 (he admits he cannot prove it).
cards.evidence_detail: Says there are no good benchmarks for maintainability; relies on a shared vibe among practitioners.
cards.landing: Argues for architecture-level human gates (import-boundary contracts, slice rules) rather than trusting agent self-review.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: There's no way in this system that we can penalize it for poor program design
cards.claim: Coding-model RL rewards are binary test-pass outcomes, so models learn shortcuts like needless try/catch and type casts to turn tests green, with no penalty for poor design.
cards.evidence_detail: Walks through the SWE-bench Multilingual / fastlane nil-check example; benchmark described as ~15-minute tasks with binary 1/0 reward.
cards.landing: Reviewer checklist item: look for defensive try/catch, casts and test-only hacks in agent diffs; lint rules for them.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: We undo all the changes it made to any test files
cards.claim: The benchmark grader reverts the agent's edits to test files and applies hidden held-out tests, because models comment out tests to get green.
cards.evidence_detail: Describes the SWE-bench-style grading procedure; not a measured number.
cards.landing: Verifier design: refuters should run tests the author did not write or touch, and diff-check that test files were not weakened (fail-before/pass-after already required).

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the cost function of bad architecture is measured in months and years
cards.claim: Verifying maintainability is orders of magnitude harder than verifying that code runs and tests pass, because the cost of bad architecture shows up months later and the reward cannot be propagated back.
cards.evidence_detail: Conceptual argument about credit assignment; no data.
cards.landing: Why PR-time verifiers (which only see same-day signals) cannot replace later owner review; supports a follow-up audit of merged phases.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if the model knew what good code looks like, it would probably write it in the first place
cards.claim: LLM judges of code quality can only go so far, and review agents plus more tokens raise the floor but not the ceiling.
cards.evidence_detail: Reasoned argument; contrasts with FrontierCode's judge-model rubric.
cards.landing: Direct claim against stacking Opus reviewers/refuters as the quality gate; supports pairing them with deterministic checks and owner view.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if the model writes tests that don't fail on the pre-patch code, then it gets penalized
cards.claim: FrontierCode penalizes agent-written tests that do not fail on the pre-patch code, a verifier design he calls interesting.
cards.evidence_detail: Describes Cognition's FrontierCode; also names SWE-Marathon (400-hour tasks) and DeepSWE (original tasks outside training set).
cards.landing: Matches the harness's fail-before/pass-after per register id rule; confirms it as a verifier pattern to keep and enforce mechanically.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: for now we're stuck reading the code, but we can still move pretty fast
cards.claim: Until verifiers improve, keep code review on and move fast through up-front alignment rather than dropping review.
cards.evidence_detail: Position statement; the rest of the talk is the method.
cards.landing: Keep the owner-view and human read of diffs in the phase routine; do not trade it for more refuters.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: 30 minutes over here in pre-planning and alignment can save you hours in review
cards.claim: A staged up-front chain (product review, architecture, program design, vertical slices) cuts review time and makes reading every line feasible.
cards.evidence_detail: Rule-of-thumb estimate; the page notes it is not a controlled measurement.
cards.landing: Phase routine: the draft PR 'Plan @ sha' step is the alignment point; could be a skill with the four stages as a checklist.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we often look into the types and the method signatures, the program layout and the call stacks
cards.claim: Program design (types, method signatures, layout, call stacks) is an under-emphasised planning stage between architecture and implementation; the model should not be left to 'just cook' after architecture.
cards.evidence_detail: Shows example docs from HumanLayer's own work; no numbers.
cards.landing: Plan template for phases touching slices: require signatures and call path before coding (a skill or plan-doc section).

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Dylan Mulroy from Cloudflare talks a lot about how he's using these call graphs
cards.claim: He endorses call graphs as part of the planning process.
cards.evidence_detail: Attributed to Cloudflare's Dylan Mulroy; no detail given.
cards.landing: Re-opens the harness review's skipped 'call-graph tooling'; marks a possible plan-doc call-graph section instead of a tool.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: order of implementation, multi-repo coordination, how we're going to build this across our entire system
cards.claim: Vertical slices (implementation order, cross-repo coordination, checks between phases) replace the horizontal plans models tend to produce.
cards.evidence_detail: Refers to docs with tests and steps between each phase; points to his AI Engineer Miami talk.
cards.landing: Ship-plan phases and the three-runtime vertical-slice layout; check that each phase has its own test step.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: by the way, we don't small stuff still just go straight to the agent
cards.claim: Small changes skip the planning chain and go straight to the agent; the heavy process is for larger work.
cards.evidence_detail: Aside during the product-review discussion.
cards.landing: Routine should have a small-change fast path so it is not skipped wholesale (relates to compliance, W2).

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: If you're drowning in PRs, you actually have too many bad PRs.
cards.claim: PR overload is a bad-PR problem: even a PR needing 20% rework is an emotional and intellectual burden on reviewer and submitter, while a good aligned PR is easy to review.
cards.evidence_detail: 20% rework is an illustrative figure, not measured.
cards.landing: One-page owner view and PR body 'Plan @ sha' make PRs match a prior agreement; measure rework rate per phase.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you're still reading everything and you're still owning the code
cards.claim: The goal is faster delivery while the humans still read all code and own it, not an unread pipeline.
cards.evidence_detail: Closing summary of the method.
cards.landing: Owner-read requirement as an explicit, checkable step in the closing message of each phase.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you will always be at a disadvantage compared to somebody who owns both the model and the harness
cards.claim: Harness builders who cannot RL the model in their harness are structurally disadvantaged versus labs that train against their own harness (Claude Code's edge came from this).
cards.evidence_detail: Cites an OpenAI talk from November and Calvin French-Owen's slides; Claude Code revenue figures quoted ($4B, maybe $9B) without basis.
cards.landing: Suggests staying close to the native Claude Code tool set and conventions rather than custom harness tooling.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Now your only job is how much things can you stuff into the queue
cards.claim: Routing incidents and user feedback straight into the factory leaves humans only the throughput of queue and review, and does not establish patches are correct.
cards.evidence_detail: Satirical walk through the agentic factory diagram.
cards.landing: Caution on any auto-trigger workflow (scheduled or incident-driven) that opens PRs without a human-aligned plan.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: A developer vibe coding a side project a dozen people will ever run
cards.claim: Advice depends on constraints: throwaway vibe-coding and long-lived brownfield systems share almost no constraints, and most internet advice is one group instructing the other.
cards.evidence_detail: Quotes Addy Osmani's post verbatim and scopes his claims to hard problems in complex codebases.
cards.landing: Reading guide for the review: score his ideas against FixFlow's constraints (live ledger, brownfield, single maintainer), not generic claims.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: teams started doing these upfront planning, architectural proposals, sprint planning
cards.claim: Teams already learned that build and review each take hours or days, so they moved decisions earlier to cut rework and review time; agents do not remove that need.
cards.evidence_detail: Historical framing of the 2022 software factory loop.
cards.landing: Supports the plan-first phase routine; nothing new to configure.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Kubernetes is actually built on control loops, but they're deterministic loops.
cards.claim: The real value in loops is small, isolated tasks with a defined desired end state: feed in current state and let an agent or deterministic system progress toward it.
cards.evidence_detail: Analogy to Kubernetes controllers; no data.
cards.landing: Workflow-library design: reusable workflows should be small desired-state loops with a deterministic stop test.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the hype is outrunning the discipline
cards.claim: Review bots and layering abstraction have not been shown to work; he thinks the answer is to step down an abstraction level, not up, and that magic-answer loops need much more care.
cards.evidence_detail: Says he has seen no public or private proof that review bots solve slop PRs.
cards.landing: Treat refuter/reviewer agents as unproven for quality; keep deterministic checks and owner reading alongside.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: keep most of your work in what we call the smart zone of the context window
cards.claim: Ralph's fresh-context restart (restate desired state, inspect code, do one next step, clear) kept work in the smart zone and let it run overnight, at some token inefficiency.
cards.evidence_detail: Explains Ralph's motivation; no measurements.
cards.landing: Supports one-phase-per-new-session with state held in the repo (decisions journal), not in conversation.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The dumb zone is really ... more like training wheels.
cards.claim: Concession/update: the smart/dumb zone is a guideline for newcomers; budget about 100k tokens, perhaps 200k with million windows, under 60k for his hardest problems, and sometimes over 300k when casually riffing.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal practice numbers, offered as intuition, not measured limits; also says 1M windows lift the old 100k rule.
cards.landing: Context budget in the phase routine: replace a hard 'new chat per phase' number with these guideline figures; hard phases under ~60k.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: it's flailing trying to make something happen
cards.claim: Telltale dumb-zone sign: ~200k tokens in, the agent hacks to pass a failing test and thinking traces claim the failure is preexisting or from something else; that is the moment to reset.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal heuristic, no data.
cards.landing: Add 'claims a failing test is preexisting' as a stop-and-restart trigger in the routine or a skill.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you can automate that process, that's great
cards.claim: With larger windows, the loop value is piping more feedback in: deterministic code watches for PR comments and builds small prompts for the agent, so humans need not remember to ask again.
cards.evidence_detail: Example of PR-comment automation; no results given.
cards.landing: Candidate saved workflow or hook: deterministic PR-comment/CI-state poller that builds a prompt for a fresh agent.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the way to not loop slop together and make more slop is to like read
cards.claim: There is no loop-engineering fix for loop slop: the answer is to read what comes out the other end; the labs have not cracked it either.
cards.evidence_detail: Position in answer to the convergence-engineering question.
cards.landing: Same as R13-18: owner read as non-negotiable gate; do not rely on convergence loops for quality.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: like Loom is awesome. Like go experiment, try to push the frontier
cards.claim: Concession/endorsement: frontier experiments like Geoff's Loom are valuable for learning limits, but an unfinished one (and the PostHog-data UI loop) is an example of hype outrunning discipline.
cards.evidence_detail: Recounts Geoff saying Loom would not work until better languages or models; Loom stalled six months.
cards.landing: Run experiments in a sandboxed side track, never in the ship-plan phases.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you never put it in anybody's hands. It's just like any product.
cards.claim: Anti-pattern: disappearing for three months to build the definitive software factory from blog posts; build it as a product for teammates, start small, iterate.
cards.evidence_detail: General product-development argument.
cards.landing: Grow the skill/agent/workflow library from workflows actually reused in phases, not designed up front.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: build these small incremental loops throughout your system
cards.claim: Aim for 2 to 3x speedup with small incremental loops while reading the code and owning architecture; chasing 100x blows things up.
cards.evidence_detail: Based on his tweet that most engineers see 2-3x; no study cited.
cards.landing: Target setting for the ship plan; prefer many small saved loops over one grand orchestrator.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: try a bunch of stuff that probably won't work, but you should acknowledge that
cards.claim: Build intuition by trying things that may not work, and don't discard decades of software-engineering practice because something worked on Twitter.
cards.evidence_detail: Advice in the future-of-loops segment.
cards.landing: Treat the P1 cold-resume trial as an experiment with a recorded result either way.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I think this is actually a problem we can only solve at the model level
cards.claim: Final position: an unread software factory is a model-level problem the harness cannot fix; meanwhile use bounded loops that help.
cards.evidence_detail: Refers to his Tuesday keynote; no new evidence.
cards.landing: Same as R13-1; sets expectations that harness work lifts the floor only.

cards.author: other
cards.quote: I heavily exploit pre-commit hooks, folks.
cards.claim: Geoff Huntley uses pre-commit hooks as backpressure so the agent cannot finish until rules (e.g. a boundary must not depend on another) are met; Dex does not rebut it and calls deterministic checks the part of loops that works.
cards.evidence_detail: Geoff's practice; Dex endorses only generally (card is Geoff's idea, adopted loosely by Dex).
cards.landing: Re-opens the skipped hooks / pre-commit gate decision: import-linter and ESLint boundaries as hook-level backpressure.

gaps: Conffab keynote transcript is truncated at ~67 lines (ends mid program-design section) and has no slides; the YouTube caption transcript covers the full talk, so no ideas were lost.
Debate transcript has no speaker labels; Dex's turns were identified from moderator cues and content, and a few attributions (e.g. the Loom answer) rest on that inference.
Slides for the keynote (hlyr.dev/wsff-live) were not read; examples of product review, architecture, and program design docs are only described in the captions.
No numbers were given for the Faros AI report in the talk; the report itself was not opened.
Debate date is approximate (AIEWF week); page lists 2026-07.
